name: Prize crossword No 24,379
preamble: 7 and 20 down play a game with 28s. Neither player has a clue, nor have any of the loose 28s. One of the players is also a 28.

clue.text: Gloomy sergeant on 8's put through the mill

blocks.note: black can mean dismal or pessimistic, as in a black mood
8 is SLEEVE, and the Beatles' Sgt Pepper is the sergeant pictured on a famous album sleeve

explanation.surface: A depressed army sergeant has been through a gruelling ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference sends you to the 8-down answer, a record sleeve; Sgt Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band is the Beatles album whose cover stars the sergeant.
explanation.definitionFit: Peppercorns are ground in a pepper mill, so the spice is literally something fed through a grinder.

clue.text: Short break in Yorkshire city when also occupying properties

indicators.note: something in a place sits inside it, so one piece is placed within another
to occupy a space is to sit inside it, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: Leeds is the largest city in West Yorkshire
as in 'as I left' means when I left
short for holiday

explanation.surface: Someone takes a brief holiday in Leeds while also living in rented property there.
explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces go into the city at different points: the word for 'when' after its first two letters, and the short holiday before its last two. 'Also' simply tells you a second insertion is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A leasehold is a property held on a lease for a fixed term, as opposed to freehold ownership.

clue.text: Sort of filter, as Aldrin was with Armstrong?

blocks.note: first meaning: a perforated bowl for draining food
second meaning, read as two parts: a fellow lander, since Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon together with Neil Armstrong

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as CO-LANDER: CO- means joint, and Aldrin shared the 1969 Apollo 11 lunar landing with Armstrong. The question mark flags the made-up word.
explanation.definitionFit: A colander is a kitchen strainer, a bowl full of holes used for draining pasta or vegetables.

clue.text: Stalag resident's radical uprising could be explosive

definitions.note: the definition is by example: gunpowder is one kind of powder

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a stalag was a German camp for prisoners of war, abbreviated POW
a red is a left-wing radical

explanation.surface: A prisoner's revolutionary revolt in a wartime camp might blow up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like the rebellion of the surface, but it only turns the radical upside down in the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunpowder is the classic explosive, so powder is something that may well go bang.

clue.text: Food writer's in bed, headto-toe with short man

indicators.note: head to toe means the top goes to the bottom, so the first letter moves to the end
something in a thing sits inside it, so one piece is placed within another
short marks a cut-down form of a name, giving its familiar abbreviation

blocks.note: the writer of the clue refers to themselves as I
taken as written, then its first letter moves to the end
Les is the short form of Leslie, a man's name

explanation.surface: A food writer lies in bed top-to-tail with a little man.
explanation.walkthrough: BED becomes EDB once its head goes to the foot; the setter's I then slips in before the B, and the man's shortened name follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Edibles is a plural noun for things fit to eat, so it can stand for food in general.

clue.text: Disc protection makes Lee very content

indicators.note: the content of something is what is inside it, so the letters are found within the words

blocks.note: the run of letters sits across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Some protection for a record or CD keeps a man called Lee happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy in the surface, but it means the contents of the preceding words.
explanation.definitionFit: A record or CD is kept in a paper or card cover that guards it from scratches and dust.

clue.text: Bag antique hidden in lobby

indicators.note: something concealed within a space is put inside it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a hall is an entrance lobby
antique means old

explanation.surface: An antique bag has been stashed away in a hotel lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden in' is not a pointer to letters lying in plain sight here; it puts the word for antique inside the lobby.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a large soft travelling bag, roomy enough to carry everything.

clue.text: Attractive extension flanks hotel

indicators.note: to flank is to stand on both sides of something, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: a wing is an extension of a building
an inn is a small hotel

explanation.surface: A handsome new wing has been built either side of a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The hotel sits inside the extension, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning smile or manner is charming and appealing, one sense of attractive.

clue.text: Monarch's implicated in articles in three languages after that

indicators.note: to be implicated in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the English definite article
Elizabeth Regina, the Queen's cipher
the French indefinite article
the German masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A king or queen has been mixed up in pieces written in three tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' are grammatical, not newspaper pieces: one each from English, French and German, in that order. ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal style thereunder means under that or in accordance with it, following on from what was stated.

clue.text: 'Mourinho hides neural problem!' in press-speak

indicators.note: a problem is something wrong or out of order, so the letters are put into a new arrangement
to hide something is to keep it inside, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: José Mourinho is the Portuguese football manager
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline about the football manager concealing a nerve condition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is itself a piece of tabloid headline writing, which is the joke: the manager's first name wraps around the rearranged word.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalese is the clichéd, sensational style of writing typical of newspapers and tabloids.

clue.text: Bletchley Park guy's rank not registered after last month

indicators.note: not means without, so a letter is taken away
coming after something means being placed behind it in the answer

blocks.note: December, the last month of the year, abbreviated
rank as in order of seniority
R is the symbol for a registered trademark

explanation.surface: A wartime code-breaker's grade is unrecorded, starting from December.
explanation.walkthrough: Bletchley Park was the British codebreaking centre in the Second World War, where Enigma was cracked. The R comes out of the rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Bletchley Park staff broke enemy ciphers, so one of its workers is someone who cracks codes.

clue.text: null
Relax in card game, adding three points

blocks.note: loo is an old card game
three compass points: south, east, north

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds over a game of cards and scores three more points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' in crosswords usually means compass points; 'in' is part of the surface picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To relax a grip or a rule is to make it less tight, which is to slacken it.

clue.text: London leads it in song as broadcast by bum?

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than seen, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: the Londonderry Air is the tune of Danny Boy; with London leading, the rest of the title follows

explanation.surface: A London tramp leads the singing on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The Londonderry Air is the Irish melody behind Danny Boy; drop the London that leads it and say the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Derriere is a jokey borrowing from French for the backside, and bum is British slang for the bottom.

clue.text: Mock scarlet-backed fish

indicators.note: backed means turned back to front, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: scarlet is a shade of red
the ide is a freshwater fish, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A fake fish with a red back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock' looks like an adjective for a fake fish, but it is the verb that defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To mock someone is to ridicule or scoff at them, which is exactly what deriding means.

clue.text: Bureaucracy got less significant, back to front

indicators.note: the back part is brought round to the front, so the end of the word is moved to its start

blocks.note: something that tapered off dwindled in importance

explanation.surface: Officialdom became less important, entirely in reverse order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' is not a letter-by-letter reversal: the word is split in two and its back half is brought round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is excessive official procedure, named after the ribbon once used to tie government documents.

clue.text: Part of oil rig Adair bent over, getting back problem

indicators.note: a thing bent over is folded so its end comes round to where it began, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: Red Adair was the famous American oil-well firefighter
a rick is a sprain or wrench, as in a ricked back

explanation.surface: A firefighter on an oil rig stoops over and hurts his back.
explanation.walkthrough: Adair stands for his nickname Red, apt on an oil rig since Red Adair capped burning oil wells; the surface's bending over is the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A derrick is the tall framework tower over an oil well that supports the drilling gear.

clue.text: Olympics boss clutches woman's stick

indicators.note: to clutch is to grip something tightly, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: Sebastian Coe chaired the organising committee for the 2012 London Olympics
the possessive her, belonging to a woman

explanation.surface: The head of the Olympic Games grabs a woman's walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' wants to be a noun from the surface, but it is the verb meaning to hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohere is to hold together or adhere, the verbal sense of stick.

clue.text: Observe present and past playground feature

blocks.note: the present tense of the verb
the past tense of the same verb

explanation.surface: Look at the playground equipment, now and in times gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' and 'past' are grammar terms: the verb is given in two tenses, one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a plank pivoted in the middle on which two children go up and down in a park.

clue.text: Old book revealed by radioactive dating

indicators.note: what is revealed by something was lying inside it waiting to be exposed

blocks.note: the run crosses the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An ancient volume has its age established by carbon dating.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about how the book's age is found; the answer is lying inside the two words that seem to describe the method.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, sacred texts composed in early Sanskrit thousands of years ago.

clue.text: Wandering preacher or critic

indicators.note: wandering means straying from a set course, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An itinerant preacher, or perhaps a critic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link offering a choice, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: One who reproaches finds fault and expresses disapproval, which is what a critic does.

clue.text: Formal dance when alien leaves formal dance

indicators.note: when someone leaves they are no longer there, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: ET is the alien from the Spielberg film
ballet is a formal, classical form of dance

explanation.surface: A grand dance occurs once the visitor from space has departed it.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'formal dance' phrases mean different things: the first is the event, the second the art form from which ET departs.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a large formal social gathering held for dancing, with evening dress.

clue.text: Catch sailor in his element - Sunday school!

indicators.note: something in a thing sits inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is the stock crossword sailor
a sailor is in his element on the sea
SS is the standard abbreviation for Sunday school

explanation.surface: A sailor feels right at home teaching at a church Sunday school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His element' refers back to the sailor, whose natural environment is the sea; the abbreviation for Sunday school then follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea bass is a fish that anglers land, so it is a catch in the fishing sense.

clue.text: Is it raised by suspicious East End intellectual?

indicators.note: London's East End is Cockney territory, where an initial H goes unspoken, so this is the word as pronounced there

blocks.note: an intellectual is a highbrow, which in Cockney speech drops its H

explanation.surface: A question asking whether a wary Cockney thinker lifts something.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys from London's East End drop their aitches, so highbrow comes out as 'ighbrow. The definition is the question itself: suspicious people raise this.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising one eyebrow is the classic facial sign of doubt or suspicion, so the question describes it.

clue.text: Feel very distressed about 13 disease

indicators.note: distressed furniture is deliberately knocked about, so these letters are roughed up into a new order
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
13-across is BLUE, and feeling blue is feeling low

explanation.surface: Someone feels terribly upset about an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feel very distressed' reads as one phrase, but it is fodder plus anagram signal; the cross-reference to the BLUE answer must be turned into its synonym before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow fever is a tropical viral infection spread by mosquitoes, named for the jaundice it causes.
